Well, yeah, I suppose so. I used to do a lot of stuff around the house. Like, I'd always be out back messing with my tomato plants. Got these Big Boys, you know? It's that cheap plastic junk they sell down at the big box stores now. Used to be they made those things out of solid brass, right? You'd buy one and it would last you twenty years. Sleep? Nah, not really waking up early. If anything, it's just hard to get out of bed at all. But waking up at the crack of dawn? No.

Yeah, every single day. It's been like this for about two weeks now, right around the time my daughter shipped out of Georgia for the military. 

Man, Fort Benning... well, Fort Moore now, I guess they changed the name. Well, looking back on it... yeah, I guess these low stretches have been coming around for about a year or so. But this one, right after my daughter shipped out, this one's hit me the absolute hardest. 

It's funny how things hit you, you know? Like when my old dog, Buster, passed away back in... must've been '18. He was a good boy, a lab mix. Found him wandering around the loading dock one morning, shivering, covered in grease. I took him home, cleaned him up with some Dawn dish soap—best thing for grease, by the way, cuts right through it. Anyway, Buster used to wait for me by the front door every single day. When he died, the house just felt... empty. Quiet. My wife, God rest her soul, she used to say that silence was golden, but I don't know about that. Sometimes silence is just loud. Like when the power goes out at the warehouse and the hum of the conveyors stops, and suddenly you can hear every little creak and groan of the metal roof. We had a blackout during that ice storm a few years back, and I had to stay overnight with a skeleton crew to make sure the pipes didn't freeze. We sat around in the breakroom with flashlights, eating stale vending machine pretzels and telling ghost stories. Old man Jenkins swore he saw a shadow moving in Aisle 4, but I told him it was just the raccoons that get in through the loading bays. Those things are smart, doc. I watched one figure out how to open a latch on a dumpster once. Just popped it right open like he had thumbs. 

But, uh, yeah. About a year I've been getting these spells. This one's just... it's a lot heavier.

Well, that's the thing, isn't it? Back to my usual self... I'm not really sure I know what that means anymore. I mean, between those heavy spells, I guess I felt... different? But not exactly like the old me.

I used to do a lot of stuff around the house. Like, I'd always be out back messing with my tomato plants. Got these Big Boys, you know? But the dirt around here is basically just pure red clay. You gotta mix in so much peat moss and compost just to get a single root to take. My neighbor, Gary, he swears by dumping eggshells and old coffee grounds in the dirt, but I keep telling him he's just setting up a buffet for the raccoons. And man, those raccoons are getting bold. Tore up my trash cans last Tuesday. Had chicken bones and junk scattered all over the driveway. Took me an hour to hose it down, and the darn hose nozzle was leaking the whole time. It's that cheap plastic junk they sell down at the big box stores now. Used to be they made those things out of solid brass, right? You'd buy one and it would last you twenty years. I just look at all that stuff—the bench, the plants, the games—and it's like it belongs to somebody else. I just don't have it in me to care about any of it right now.\n\nDoctor: Have you been waking up much earlier than usual and unable to get back to sleep?\n\nPatient: Sleep? Nah, not really waking up early. If anything, it's just hard to get out of bed at all. But waking up at the crack of dawn? Had a couple thousand guys in suits sweating through their shirts. They tried bringing in these giant industrial fans, but all that did was blow hot, humid air around like a giant hair dryer. And the catering! Don't even get me started on the catering. They served us this lukewarm chicken salad that had been sitting out, and half the management team from the Atlanta branch spent the next two days fighting over the bathrooms at the Holiday Inn. I stuck to the crackers and ginger ale, thank God. You gotta be careful with mayonnaise-based stuff when the temperature gets above eighty degrees, everybody knows that. It's just common sense. But these corporate event planners, they don't think about logistics, they just look at the price per head...\n\nWait, sorry doc. I'm doing it again, aren't I? Yeah, it's been every day for the last two weeks, ever since she left.\n\nDoctor: Over the past two weeks, have you been having trouble concentrating?\n\nPatient: Yeah, concentration's been... it's been real tough. Wired? Yeah, actually... there was a stretch a while back where I had just so much energy I didn't know what to do with it. I was waking up way before daylight. I mean, pitch black outside, the birds aren't even up yet, and I'm wide awake at the kitchen table, drawing up all these big plans for changes at the warehouse. I finally got it patched up just in time for summer. Isn't that how it always goes? 

I ended up selling it to a guy a few towns over, and I still kick myself for it. I saw it parked outside a diner maybe five years later, and the guy had painted it this awful matte black. Looked like a chalkboard on wheels. It's a crime what some people do to classic vehicles. Just absolutely no respect for the original engineering. 

But, uh... yeah. I was just going and going, jumping from project to project. Didn't want to stop for a second.

A full week? I don't know, maybe? Like I said, I wasn't really keeping track of time. 

Time is a funny thing, though, isn't it? My grandfather used to have this grandfather clock in his hallway. Beautiful piece of woodwork, mahogany, I think. Or maybe cherry. Anyway, he had to wind it every single Sunday with this brass key. If he forgot, the whole thing would just stop dead on Tuesday afternoon. I remember being fascinated by the pendulum swinging back and forth. Tick, tock, tick, tock. 

He actually taught me how to tell time on that clock. None of this digital stuff they teach kids today. You had to know where the big hand and the little hand were. He gave me his old pocket watch when I turned twelve. An Elgin, silver case, real heavy in your hand. I carried it everywhere until I dropped it in a puddle down by the creek. The crystal smashed, water got inside, ruined the whole mechanism. Took it to a watchmaker downtown, guy named Mr. Henderson. He had this little magnifying glass squeezed into his eye, looked like a cyborg or something. He took one look at it and shook his head. Said it would cost more to fix than it was worth. 

I still have it, though, sitting in a drawer somewhere in the bedroom. Next to my old high school class ring. The stone fell out of that ring years ago. It was supposed to be a ruby, but I'm pretty sure it was just red glass. You know how those things are, they charge you an arm and a leg for a piece of cheap metal...

But yeah, a week? Longer? I really couldn't say for sure. It just felt like one long, fast stretch.

Yeah, I guess you could say that. Before this whole low spell hit, I was feeling way too fired up. Like everything was finally going my way, you know? Or, well, either that or I was snapping at folks over small things I'd normally just let slide. 

Speaking of snapping, my neighbor's dog—that little terrier mix I mentioned?—it snapped at the mail carrier last week. Just lunged right at his ankle while he was trying to put the mail in the box. The mail carrier is this younger guy, always wears those shorts, even when it's freezing out. I don't know how he does it. My knees ache if the temperature drops below fifty. I tried wearing those copper compression sleeves they sell on TV, the ones with the retired quarterback doing the commercial? Total waste of money. Might as well have wrapped my knees in tin foil. 

Anyway, the mail guy had to use his bag as a shield. The dog didn't break the skin, but the neighbor still had to come out and apologize. Brought the mail guy a gift card to the coffee shop down the street. That coffee shop used to be a hardware store when I was growing up. Old man Miller ran it. You could walk in there and buy a single nail if you wanted to. Try doing that at one of these big box stores today. They make you buy a box of five hundred, and they're all made of cheap pot metal that bends as soon as you hit it with a hammer. 

I was building a birdhouse a few years back and went through half a box of those cheap nails just trying to get the roof attached. Finally gave up and used wood glue. Gorilla glue, actually. That stuff expands like crazy. I got some on my thumb and it took me a week to peel it off. Felt like I was shedding my skin like a snake...

But, uh, yeah. Feeling good, feeling fired up, or just getting irritated real easy. That's how it was.

But she went down there, and I told her, I said, \"You better get used to the heat, kiddo, because South Georgia in the summer is like walking on the surface of the sun.\" I remember when I was down near Columbus for a distribution conference back in '09. We were supposed to be looking at these new automated conveyor systems, but the AC in the expo hall completely crapped out on the first day. Had a couple thousand guys in suits sweating through their shirts. They tried bringing in these giant industrial fans, but all that did was blow hot, humid air around like a giant hair dryer. And the catering! Don't even get me started on the catering. They served us this lukewarm chicken salad that had been sitting out, and half the management team from the Atlanta branch spent the next two days fighting over the bathrooms at the Holiday Inn. I stuck to the crackers and ginger ale, thank God. You gotta be careful with mayonnaise-based stuff when the temperature gets above eighty degrees, everybody knows that. It's just common sense. But these corporate event planners, they don't think about logistics, they just look at the price per head...\n\nWait, sorry doc. I'm doing it again, aren't I? You asked about how long I've been feeling heavy. Yeah, it's been every day for the last two weeks, ever since she left.\n\nDoctor: Over the past two weeks, have you been having trouble concentrating?\n\nPatient: Yeah, concentration's been... it's been real tough. At the distribution center, I'll be sitting there staring at the schedule or the routing sheet, and my mind just won't lock in. You know? It's like I'm looking at the words, but they aren't meaning anything. And then I get these little staffing calls, guys calling out sick or whatever, and it feels like this massive problem I gotta solve, way bigger than it ought to be. \n\nUsually I can handle that stuff in my sleep. I mean, staffing a warehouse ain't rocket science, but you gotta know your people. Like Tommy on the loading dock, you can't put him with Martinez because they'll just argue about college football the whole shift. Martinez is a die-hard Bulldogs fan, right? Got the bumper sticker, the hat, probably got a bulldog tattooed on his backside for all I know. And Tommy, he went to Auburn for like a semester back in the nineties before he dropped out, but he still acts like he's on the coaching staff. They get into it over the dumbest things. Last year, Martinez actually threw a roll of packing tape at Tommy's head because of some call a referee made in a game that happened five years ago. I had to write them both up. HR wanted me to send them to some conflict resolution seminar downtown, but I told them, \"Look, you put these two in a room with a whiteboard and a therapist, and somebody's gonna end up going through a window.\" Corporate HR, they don't get the warehouse culture. They think everybody communicates with \"I feel\" statements. If I walked onto the floor and started talking about my feelings, they'd laugh me right out of the building. You gotta talk to these guys on their level, you know? Firm, but fair. \n\nBut, uh... yeah. Staring at the schedule. My brain's just in a fog lately. Can't focus on it at all.\n\nDoctor: Before these last two weeks, have you ever had another period like this in your life?\n\nPatient: Well, looking back on it... yeah, I guess these low stretches have been coming around for about a year or so. But this one, right after my daughter shipped out, this one's hit me the absolute hardest. \n\nIt's funny how things hit you, you know? Like when my old dog, Buster, passed away back in... must've been '18. He was a good boy, a lab mix. Found him wandering around the loading dock one morning, shivering, covered in grease. I took him home, cleaned him up with some Dawn dish soap—best thing for grease, by the way, cuts right through it. Anyway, Buster used to wait for me by the front door every single day. When he died, the house just felt... empty. Quiet. My wife, God rest her soul, she used to say that silence was golden, but I don't know about that. Sometimes silence is just loud. Like when the power goes out at the warehouse and the hum of the conveyors stops, and suddenly you can hear every little creak and groan of the metal roof. We had a blackout during that ice storm a few years back, and I had to stay overnight with a skeleton crew to make sure the pipes didn't freeze. We sat around in the breakroom with flashlights, eating stale vending machine pretzels and telling ghost stories. Old man Jenkins swore he saw a shadow moving in Aisle 4, but I told him it was just the raccoons that get in through the loading bays. Those things are smart, doc. I watched one figure out how to open a latch on a dumpster once. Just popped it right open like he had thumbs. \n\nBut, uh, yeah. About a year I've been getting these spells. This one's just... it's a lot heavier.\n\nDoctor: Before this current stretch, did you ever have another period lasting at least two weeks when you felt this same heavy way nearly every day?\n\nPatient: Yeah, like I was saying, it's... it's been about a year or so that these low stretches have been coming around. They'd last a couple weeks, maybe a little longer, where I'd just feel that same heaviness every day. But this one right now, after my daughter shipped out, this is the hardest it's ever hit me. \n\nIt's strange how time works, though, isn't it? A year sounds like a long time, but it goes by in a blink. I remember when I first started at the warehouse, I thought I'd be there for maybe six months, just until I found something better. That was thirty years ago! Thirty years. I've seen guys come and go, seen the whole industry change. We used to do everything on paper, carbon copies. You had to press so hard with your pen your hand would cramp up by noon. Now it's all barcodes and scanners and computers that tell you exactly where everything is. Supposed to make it easier, but half the time the system goes down and nobody knows what to do because they don't know how to read a manifest anymore. I had a kid last week, couldn't have been more than nineteen, staring at a pallet of auto parts like it was an alien spaceship just because his scanner battery died. I told him, \"Son, before you were born, we moved twice as much freight with half the technology.\" But they don't teach them how to think on their feet anymore. It's all just following the beep. \n\nBut yeah, anyway... to answer your question, doc, I've had periods like this for about a year, but nothing quite this heavy.\n\nDoctor: Between these low stretches over the past year, did you ever get completely back to feeling like your usual self?\n\nPatient: Well, that's the thing, isn't it? Back to my usual self... I'm not really sure I know what that means anymore. I mean, between those heavy spells, I guess I felt... different? But not exactly like the old me. \n\nYou know, the old me used to rebuild carburetors on the weekend. Just for fun! Me and my buddy Sal, we'd get a twelve-pack of Miller Lite and just tear into an engine block in his garage. Sal had this incredible setup, pegboards covering every wall, every wrench outlined in black marker so you knew exactly where it went. He was a stickler for organization, Sal was. Worked as a machinist for Boeing for twenty years before he retired. He used to say, \"A place for everything, and everything in its place.\" We rebuilt a '69 Mustang once, cherry red. Took us three years. We had to source the original parts from all over the country. Found a guy in New Mexico who had a pristine original steering wheel just sitting in a barn. Can you believe that? A barn! Covered in dust and chicken feathers, but underneath it was perfect. We drove out there in Sal's pickup, straight through, taking turns at the wheel. Ate nothing but beef jerky and gas station hot dogs the whole way. I tell you, my stomach wasn't right for a week after that, but man, the open road... there's nothing like it. Just the hum of the tires and the radio playing classic rock. \n\nBut, uh... what were we talking about? Oh, right. Feeling normal. Yeah, I don't know if I ever really got back to normal between those low times. It's hard to say.\n\nDoctor: For the past two years, have you felt down or heavy more days than not?\n\nPatient: Two years? Uh... well, I don't know about two whole years. Like I said, it's been about a year or so with these spells, but before that... I don't really think I felt heavy most days. Two years ago... man, two years ago was when I finally broke down and bought that John Deere riding mower. \n\nMy knees were just giving out pushing that old Toro around the yard. Best investment I ever made, doc. It has that zero-turn radius, you know? You can spin on a dime right around the big oak tree in the front yard. And a cup holder! You wouldn't think a cup holder on a lawnmower is a big deal, but let me tell you, on a hot July afternoon with an ice-cold sweet tea... it is heaven. My neighbor Gary, he has this little electric push mower. Sounds exactly like a giant hair dryer. And he leaves his grass clippings right on the sidewalk. Drives me absolutely crazy. I always tell him he needs to sweep that up before it washes into the storm drain, but he just looks at me like I am speaking Greek. \n\nPeople these days just do not take pride in their property. You drive down my street, and half the houses have gutters overflowing with pine needles. I clean mine out twice a year, regular as clockwork. I even got a special attachment for the hose. It blasts the muck right out of there. You have to be careful on the ladder, though. One of the guys at the warehouse, Tommy, fell off a ladder last spring and shattered his collarbone. Just a freak accident, but he was out of work for months. We had to shuffle the whole shift schedule around to cover his loading dock. \n\nBut, uh... wait, I lost my train of thought. What were you asking me? Something about two years?\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually energized or wired for several days in a row, much more than your normal self?\n\nPatient: Wired? Yeah, actually... there was a stretch a while back where I had just so much energy I didn't know what to do with it. I was waking up way before daylight. I mean, pitch black outside, the birds aren't even up yet, and I'm wide awake at the kitchen table, drawing up all these big plans for changes at the warehouse. Figured out a whole new way to route the forklifts. Then I'd be out in the freezing cold cleaning the garage, just jumping from one job to the next without even wanting to stop. \n\nWhile I was out there in the garage, I actually found my original Craftsman socket set. Buried under a tarp behind the snowblower. Let me tell you, they do not make tools like that anymore. Now it's all cheap metal from overseas that strips out the second you put any real torque on it. But this old Craftsman set, it's heavy. You can feel the quality in your hand. My dad bought me that set when I got my first truck, an '82 Chevy C10. Two-tone blue and silver. God, I loved that truck. The heater core blew out the second winter I had it, and I had to drive to work wrapped in a wool blanket for three months because I couldn't afford the parts to fix it. I finally got it patched up just in time for summer. Isn't that how it always goes? \n\nI ended up selling it to a guy a few towns over, and I still kick myself for it. I saw it parked outside a diner maybe five years later, and the guy had painted it this awful matte black. Looked like a chalkboard on wheels. It's a crime what some people do to classic vehicles. Just absolutely no respect for the original engineering. \n\nBut, uh... yeah. I was just going and going, jumping from project to project. Didn't want to stop for a second.\n\nDoctor: During that energized stretch, did you need much less sleep than usual and still feel rested?\n\nPatient: Sleep? Yeah, I guess so. I mean, like I said, I was up before the sun even thought about rising. Four hours, maybe five, and I was just ready to go. Didn't feel tired at all, honestly. Just... boom, eyes open, mind racing. \n\nIt's funny you mention sleep, though, because normally I'm a solid eight-hour guy. Have to be, right? But my wife, she's a terrible sleeper. Always has been. She bought this weighted blanket last Christmas because she saw it on one of those morning shows. Thing weighs like twenty pounds. I tried it once and felt like I was being buried alive. I don't know how she stands it. She says it makes her feel secure, but to me, it's just a trap. If there's a fire in the middle of the night, you're going to spend five minutes just trying to wrestle your way out from under that thing. \n\nWe actually had a small fire in the kitchen a few years back. The toaster oven shorted out. Scared the living daylights out of me. I had to use the extinguisher we kept under the sink, the one with the dry chemical stuff. Man, that powder gets absolutely everywhere. It took us weeks to clean it out of the grout on the backsplash. We ended up having to hire a professional cleaning crew because my wife's asthma started acting up from all the dust. The guy who came out to do the cleaning, Hector, he was a real character. Told us he used to be a rodeo clown down in Texas before he moved up here. Can you imagine that? Staring down a two-ton bull for a living. Takes a special kind of crazy, if you ask me. \n\nBut, uh... wait. What were we talking about? Oh, the sleep thing. Yeah, I didn't need much sleep at all during that stretch. Just felt totally rested and ready to tackle the day.\n\nDoctor: During that energized stretch, did it cause serious problems at work, at home, or with other people?\n\nPatient: Problems? Yeah, I guess you could say that. At home, I just completely let things go. Bills and responsibilities just piled up on the kitchen counter instead of me handling them like I normally would. I'm usually a stickler for getting the water bill paid the day it comes in. \n\nSpeaking of the mail, our regular mailman, Dave, retired last month. Guy walked that route for twenty-five years. Calves the size of bowling balls. Now we have this new kid, can't be older than twenty, and he keeps putting our neighbor's mail in our box. I mean, the numbers are right there on the side of the house in brass. Four-inch brass numbers I bought at the hardware store. I had to drill right into the brick to mount them. Broke two masonry bits doing it, too. Brick is funny like that, you hit a hard spot and it just snaps the bit right off. You have to keep the drill perfectly straight or you're just asking for trouble. \n\nBut anyway, yeah, the bills just sat there. And at work, it got pretty messy, too. I was going so fast that my mistakes got really serious. It got bad enough that one of the supervisors actually found me sitting out in my truck before dawn one morning and ended up getting occupational health involved. \n\nI was parked out under this big halogen light by the loading docks. I always park there to keep the catalytic converter thieves away. You know they can saw one of those off in under two minutes? Happened to my brother-in-law's car right in his own driveway. Just zip with a battery-powered Sawzall and they're gone into the night. Costs two grand to replace, and the insurance companies fight you tooth and nail on it. Anyway, they sent this occupational health lady down with a clipboard and everything to talk to me. She had these reading glasses on a little beaded chain around her neck. Reminded me exactly of my middle school librarian, Mrs. Gable. Mrs. Gable used to catch me trying to sneak out of study hall to go to the auto shop... \n\nWait, I'm rambling again. Did that answer what you were asking about the problems?\n\nDoctor: During that energized stretch, did you ever hear or see things other people couldn’t, or believe something others said wasn’t true?\n\nPatient: Hear or see things? No, no, nothing like that. I wasn't seeing ghosts or anything. My mind was just going a mile a minute, you know? \n\nSpeaking of seeing things, though, you wouldn't believe the deer we've had in the yard lately. Huge bucks, right up by the back patio. My wife planted these hostas last spring, spent a fortune on them at that nursery out on Route 9. The one with the big fiberglass cow on the roof? They've had that cow up there since I was a kid. Anyway, the deer treat those hostas like a salad bar. Just munch them right down to the dirt. I tried putting up some of that netting, the black plastic stuff, but it's a real pain to work with. Gets tangled on every little branch and twig. I ended up wrapping it around my own ankle and nearly took a header into the birdbath. \n\nThat birdbath is solid concrete, too. Weighs a ton. Had to use a hand truck to get it from the driveway to the backyard when we bought it. The wheels on the hand truck were a little low on air, and one of them popped right off the rim when I hit a root. Sounded like a gunshot. The neighbor's dog started barking, this little terrier mix that never shuts up... \n\nBut, uh, no. No seeing things or hearing voices or anything crazy like that. Just the energy.\n\nDoctor: About how many days in a row did that energized stretch last?\n\nPatient: How many days? Hmm, I'm not really sure, to be honest. I didn't exactly have a calendar out marking it down. \n\nSpeaking of calendars, did you know they stopped giving those out at the auto parts store? Used to be, every December, you'd go in for a couple quarts of oil and they'd hand you one of those big glossy calendars with the classic cars on them. I had a whole collection going in the garage. 1969 Mustangs, '57 Chevys, you name it. Now? Nothing. They say it's all digital now, everybody just uses their phones. But you can't hang a phone on a pegboard above your workbench, can you? \n\nI spent all last weekend trying to organize that workbench. It's a disaster area. I've got coffee cans full of screws and nails that I've been saving since the Clinton administration. You never know when you're going to need a two-inch wood screw, right? But the problem is, I don't label the cans. So I spend twenty minutes dumping out Folgers cans just looking for one specific washer. My wife bought me one of those plastic organizer bins with the little drawers, but I don't trust the plastic. Seems flimsy. Drop a hammer on that thing and it'll shatter into a million pieces. \n\nI actually did drop a hammer on my toe once. A framing hammer, the heavy kind with the waffle face on the head. Right on the big toe. Turned purple instantly. I had to drill a hole in the nail with a tiny drill bit just to relieve the pressure... \n\nWait, what were we talking about? The days? Yeah, I really couldn't tell you an exact number. It just sort of all blurred together while I was going so fast.\n\nDoctor: Did that energized stretch last a full week or longer?\n\nPatient: A full week? I don't know, maybe? Like I said, I wasn't really keeping track of time. \n\nTime is a funny thing, though, isn't it? My grandfather used to have this grandfather clock in his hallway. Beautiful piece of woodwork, mahogany, I think. Or maybe cherry. Anyway, he had to wind it every single Sunday with this brass key. If he forgot, the whole thing would just stop dead on Tuesday afternoon. I remember being fascinated by the pendulum swinging back and forth. Tick, tock, tick, tock. \n\nHe actually taught me how to tell time on that clock. None of this digital stuff they teach kids today. You had to know where the big hand and the little hand were. He gave me his old pocket watch when I turned twelve. An Elgin, silver case, real heavy in your hand. I carried it everywhere until I dropped it in a puddle down by the creek. The crystal smashed, water got inside, ruined the whole mechanism. Took it to a watchmaker downtown, guy named Mr. Henderson. He had this little magnifying glass squeezed into his eye, looked like a cyborg or something. He took one look at it and shook his head. Said it would cost more to fix than it was worth. \n\nI still have it, though, sitting in a drawer somewhere in the bedroom. Next to my old high school class ring. The stone fell out of that ring years ago. It was supposed to be a ruby, but I'm pretty sure it was just red glass. You know how those things are, they charge you an arm and a leg for a piece of cheap metal...\n\nBut yeah, a week? Longer? I really couldn't say for sure. It just felt like one long, fast stretch.\n\nDoctor: During that high-energy stretch, did you feel unusually good or on top of the world?\n\nPatient: Yeah, I guess you could say that. Before this whole low spell hit, I was feeling way too fired up. Like everything was finally going my way, you know? Or, well, either that or I was snapping at folks over small things I'd normally just let slide. \n\nSpeaking of snapping, my neighbor's dog—that little terrier mix I mentioned?—it snapped at the mail carrier last week. Just lunged right at his ankle while he was trying to put the mail in the box. The mail carrier is this younger guy, always wears those shorts, even when it's freezing out. I don't know how he does it. My knees ache if the temperature drops below fifty. I tried wearing those copper compression sleeves they sell on TV, the ones with the retired quarterback doing the commercial? Total waste of money. Might as well have wrapped my knees in tin foil. \n\nAnyway, the mail guy had to use his bag as a shield. The dog didn't break the skin, but the neighbor still had to come out and apologize. Brought the mail guy a gift card to the coffee shop down the street. That coffee shop used to be a hardware store when I was growing up. Old man Miller ran it. You could walk in there and buy a single nail if you wanted to. Try doing that at one of these big box stores today. They make you buy a box of five hundred, and they're all made of cheap pot metal that bends as soon as you hit it with a hammer. \n\nI was building a birdhouse a few years back and went through half a box of those cheap nails just trying to get the roof attached. Finally gave up and used wood glue. Gorilla glue, actually. That stuff expands like crazy. I got some on my thumb and it took me a week to peel it off. Felt like I was shedding my skin like a snake...\n\nBut, uh, yeah. Feeling good, feeling fired up, or just getting irritated real easy. That's how it was."
